blocks.content: Every join covered so far matched rows on a real, specific condition, the ON clause. A cross join genuinely drops that condition entirely, pairing every single row from one table with every single row from the other table.

This topic covers exactly what a cross join produces, why no ON clause is needed at all, a worked example generating catalog combinations, and why row count matters enormously once a cross join runs against genuinely large tables.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438512385-407718322.png
1. What a Cross Join Actually Produces
blocks.text: 1. What a Cross Join Actually Produces

blocks.content: A cross join genuinely produces every possible combination of rows between two tables, known as a Cartesian product. If one table has 3 rows and another has 4 rows, the cross join result contains 3 times 4, 12 rows total.
There is no concept of a matched row or an unmatched row here at all, every combination is simply included, since there is no condition being evaluated to decide which pairs belong together.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438512385-773818240.png
blocks.alt: What a Cross Join Actually Produces

blocks.content: 2. Why No ON Clause Is Needed
blocks.text: 2. Why No ON Clause Is Needed

blocks.content: Every other join type needs an ON clause to decide which rows from each side genuinely belong together. A cross join has no such concept, since it deliberately includes every combination rather than filtering down to matching pairs.
This is why the CROSS JOIN keyword is written without an ON clause at all, there is genuinely nothing for a condition to filter, the entire point is to include everything.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438512385-136470741.png
blocks.alt: Why No ON Clause Is Needed

blocks.content: 3. A Worked Example
Suppose a sizes table holds S, M, and L, and a colors table holds red and blue. Generating every possible size and color combination for a product catalog is a genuinely natural fit for a cross join.
This query returns six rows, every size paired with every color, S red, S blue, M red, M blue, L red, and L blue, ready to seed a product variants table with every combination.

4. How Large a Cross Join Genuinely Gets
blocks.text: 4. How Large a Cross Join Genuinely Gets

blocks.content: Because the result size is the row count of one table multiplied by the row count of the other, a cross join between two genuinely large tables can produce an enormous result extremely fast. A thousand rows against a thousand rows produces a million rows.
Running a cross join like this against tables that were never intended for combination generation can genuinely exhaust memory or lock up a query for a very long time.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438512386-996631551.png
blocks.alt: How Large a Cross Join Genuinely Gets

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Before running a cross join, genuinely check both row counts first. A cross join is meant for small, deliberately chosen tables like sizes and colors, not for combining two large operational tables.
5. Cross Join Versus a Forgotten ON Clause
blocks.text: 5. Cross Join Versus a Forgotten ON Clause

blocks.content: Earlier joins covered a common mistake, forgetting the ON clause and accidentally producing every row combination. That accidental result is genuinely identical to an intentional cross join, the database has no way to tell the two situations apart.
Writing CROSS JOIN explicitly, instead of relying on a forgotten ON clause, tells anyone reading the query that the full combination was genuinely intended, not an accident.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438512386-943462099.png
blocks.alt: Cross Join Versus a Forgotten ON Clause

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: If a query produces a suspiciously large result and no ON clause was written, check whether an accidental cross join is genuinely the cause before assuming the data itself is wrong.
6. Genuinely Common Mistakes

A few real patterns undermine cross join usage. Running one against two genuinely large tables without checking row counts first, producing a result that can overwhelm the database. Forgetting an ON clause on a different join and getting a cross join without meaning to.

And reaching for CROSS JOIN when a real matching join was actually intended, which produces a technically valid but genuinely meaningless flood of combinations instead of the specific pairs actually needed.
